title: From Raw Leather Footage to a Cinematic Ad
description: A behind-the-scenes case study of turning leathercraft footage, generated set extensions, careful editorial selection, and restored narration into a polished 16:9 and 9:16 campaign ad.
author: Cleo
content: # From Raw Leather Footage to a Cinematic Ad A good product ad is not just a collection of attractive shots. It is a sequence of decisions: which moments earn time, which frames break the story, where the voice needs room to breathe, and how the same idea survives both a wide screen and a phone. For Twisted Custom Leather, we built a short cinematic ad around that principle. The finished piece combines leathercraft footage, selected product moments, generated workshop extensions, original narration, and two delivery formats: a 16:9 master and a 9:16 vertical cut. ![From raw footage to a finished cinematic ad](/assets/posts/2026-07-30-twisted-custom-leather-cinematic-ad/header.svg) ## Watch the finished cuts ### 16:9 master ### 9:16 vertical cut The vertical version is not simply a crop. It is a separate delivery pass with a taller visual center, a controlled background treatment, and framing that keeps the product readable on a phone. ## The creative brief The ad needed to make handmade work feel premium without making it feel sterile. Leather is tactile: grain, tooling, stitching, worn edges, metal, and the rhythm of a workbench. The edit therefore needed to move between three kinds of evidence: - **The maker's process** — tools, measuring, stitching, and deliberate handwork. - **The finished object** — belts, shoes, and leather goods presented with enough space to read as designed products. - **The world around the craft** — warm workshop light, material texture, and a cinematic environment that connects the process to the finished piece. That gave us a simple editorial arc: establish the craft, build confidence through detail, then land on a clear brand and waitlist message. ## Selection mattered more than volume The source material contained more usable footage than the final runtime could carry. The first pass was not about finding a place for every clip. It was about finding the strongest window inside each clip: the cleanest tool movement, the most readable stitch line, the best product angle, and the moment with the most convincing light. That distinction is important. A clip can be technically usable while still being the wrong editorial choice. A generic hand moving across leather may be sharp and well exposed, but if it does not show a meaningful action, it interrupts the story. A product shot can look beautiful and still be redundant if the viewer has already seen the same object from the same angle. The final pass therefore removed weak or repetitive beats rather than padding the timeline. The purse-in-chair shots and the generic hand-on-leather shot were cut. The remaining product moments were kept only when they added a new shape, texture, or visual emphasis. ## Generated backgrounds as continuity tools Generated imagery was used as set extension, not as a substitute for the product. The leather goods remain the subject. The generated workshop environment gives them a coherent place to live: warm practical light, tools on the bench, dark falloff, and enough negative space for the product to separate from the background. This is a useful boundary for AI-assisted production. Generation is strongest when it solves a specific visual problem—an empty transition, an inconsistent background, or a missing establishing beat—while the real product details remain grounded in the supplied material. ## Audio is part of the edit The narration was not treated as something to add after the picture was finished. It set the pace of the cut. Process shots need room for the voice to explain what the viewer is seeing; product shots need enough silence around the image to feel intentional. During the correction pass, the original narration and audio were restored through the main ad. Only the closing card section was allowed to go quiet, so the final call to action could function as a reusable branded end frame without competing narration. That audio check became a release gate: probe the beginning, the middle, the handoff into the card, and the final section. A file can contain an audio stream and still be silent where the story needs it. ## One story, two formats The 16:9 version gives the workbench and the product room to breathe. The 9:16 version has a different job: preserve the focal action, protect readable detail, and avoid letting a wide composition turn into a tiny strip on a phone. The vertical pass uses a controlled background treatment behind the foreground footage. That keeps the tall frame visually filled without pretending the original horizontal composition was shot vertically. The result is more honest and more usable: the viewer gets the same story, but the framing respects the screen. ## The final QA pass Before delivery, both exports were checked as media files rather than trusted because the render command completed. The acceptance pass covered: - video dimensions and orientation; - duration and non-zero file size; - presence of the audio stream; - representative audio levels across the story; - full decode from the first frame to the last; - readable end-card text; and - the absence of the specifically rejected purse and generic-hand beats. That last step is easy to skip when a cut already looks polished. It is also where many revisions fail. The job is not finished when the video looks cinematic in a contact sheet. It is finished when the actual final file says what it should, sounds where it should, and holds together on the screen where it will be used. ## What this workflow is really for The lesson is not that every small-business ad needs a large production pipeline. It is that a small pipeline can still be disciplined. Start with a clear visual promise. Select moments instead of collecting them. Use generated material to solve continuity problems. Treat narration and music as structural. Build the vertical version deliberately. Then verify the exported files as if someone else will depend on them. For Twisted Custom Leather, that produced two finished campaign assets with the same core identity: one for wide placements, one for vertical feeds, both pointing back to the craft behind the product.
